\vspace{12pt}

In bout five years, the number of electric vehicles on Springfield's roads has grown nearly
sevenfold, from 320 to 2,180. Yet the city's public charging network has not kept pace.
One district, Riverside, has 120 electric cars and not a single public charger. Another,
Downtown, has 420 electric cars competing for just 12 chargers. This is the gap our team
was hired to close. GreenCharge asked us three questions: where is the demand greatest,
where should the first stations go, and how should the network grow over the next five
years.

We answer all three questions with a single framework built from the city's own data.
To measure demand, we estimate how often registered EVs require public charging and
when those visits occur. We assume stable charging habits within each district, so
expected visits grow in proportion to its registered fleet. A queue simulation then
measures how additional chargers reduce waiting and increase completed charging visits.
TOPSIS combines waiting savings and additional revenue into a priority score between
0 and 100.

To select station locations and opening phases, we evaluate complete construction
schedules whose first phase contains four to six sites within a two-million-dollar budget. Each schedule is assessed by the service and
revenue it provides, accounting for existing chargers and the capacity of the new sites.
The district graph identifies central and peripheral areas and allows us to evaluate
the effect of requiring a station in a highly connected district.

To plan the future, we forecast electric-vehicle growth with a time-series model. This
model extends the recent growth trend rather than imposing a fixed curve, and it projects
about 3,200 vehicles by 2025 and 11,900 by 2030. These forecasts increase the charging
demand entering the same service model. Financial break-even screens investment viability
before the joint search evaluates opening each candidate site in one of three phases, or leaving it unbuilt.
After Phase 1, expansion has no fixed budget ceiling; later investments must be
financially beneficial.

Our framework compares up to $4^{10}$ complete schedules and evaluates the trade-off
between service improvement and revenue. A queue may grow during a peak and recover
later; vehicles still waiting remain part of the demand account. This allows an
affordable plan to be evaluated even when it cannot immediately eliminate congestion.
The financial benchmark identifies how much service a new station must support to
cover annualized installation and maintenance costs. Together, these calculations
provide the basis for a phased recommendation to the Mayor.

\vspace{8pt}\hrule\vspace{3pt}
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} electric vehicle charging; queue simulation; TOPSIS;
demand forecasting; financial break-even; graph connectivity; phased deployment.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Background and Real-World Motivation}

Transportation is the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in most American cities,
and the fastest available lever for cutting those emissions is electrification. Springfield
has committed to a 50\% reduction in carbon emissions by 2030, and converting its
vehicle fleet to electricity is the stated centerpiece of that plan. The commitment is
already visible in the data: the city's electric-vehicle (EV) registrations grew from 320
in 2019 to 2,180 in 2024, a nearly sevenfold increase over five years.

The public charging network, however, has not grown in step. Across the nine districts,
existing public chargers number in the single digits, and one district, Riverside, has
none at all. This mismatch matters because public charging is a prerequisite for adoption.
Drivers who cannot charge at home, such as apartment residents, commuters, and commercial
fleets, postpone or abandon EV purchases when public chargers are scarce. The deployment of
charging stations is not a passive response to demand; it is a driver of demand.
Getting the placement right accelerates the city's climate goals. Getting it wrong strands
investment in underused locations.

The Mayor's Office has asked our team to design this network deliberately. The task is
inherently quantitative: demand is unevenly distributed across districts, candidate sites
differ in cost and capacity, and the network must grow over time as adoption spreads.
These features make the problem a natural fit for formal optimization and evaluation
methods.

\subsection{Problem Restatement}

We address four connected tasks. (1) Assess where current charging demand is concentrated
by identifying the factors that drive demand and ranking the nine districts by a computed
demand-priority score. (2) Select the optimal first-phase set of four to six charging
stations from ten candidate sites under a two-million-dollar installation budget, so that
the combined benefit of reduced waiting and additional charging revenue is maximized.
(3) Analyze the connectivity of the district
network and use the results, together with a forecast of EV growth, to build a phased
deployment roadmap from 2025 to 2030. (4) Deliver a plain-language recommendation report
to the Mayor and City Council.

Each task fixes the method we use: charging-demand and queue simulation with TOPSIS
for construction benefits, ARIMA for the EV forecast, and exhaustive enumeration for
phased site selection. Financial break-even connects the service model to expansion
viability. These methods connect the tasks into one framework.

\section{Charging Demand and Investment Benefits}
\subsection{Estimating Public-Charging Visits}
\label{sec:visits}
To estimate the demand that public chargers must serve, we convert the registered fleet
into expected weekly visits. We assume EVs generate public-charging demand in their
registration district and retain stable average charging habits. This local assignment
avoids estimating commuting destinations without travel data. With $E_{i,y}$ registered
EVs and $\nu_i$ public visits per EV per week, expected demand is
\begin{equation}
V_{i,y}=E_{i,y}\nu_i.\label{eq:visits}
\end{equation}
Here $\nu_i$ is the average number of public visits per registered EV per week. Holding $\nu_i$ fixed makes expected public visits directly proportional to registrations
within a district. This assumption supplies the demand volume for both waiting and
revenue; districts may have different charging frequencies.

Charging frequency depends on how far people drive and how much driving range they
replace per visit. Let $d_i$ be weekly driving distance, $L_i$ effective full-battery
range, $\delta_i$ the typical fraction of battery capacity replenished, and $q_i$ the
fraction of charging visits made at public stations. Assuming comparable energy per
visit when converting total visits to public visits, we estimate
\begin{equation}
\nu_i=\frac{q_i d_i}{L_i\delta_i},\qquad
V_{i,y}=E_{i,y}\frac{q_i d_i}{L_i\delta_i}.\label{eq:frequency}
\end{equation}
This connects demand to travel and charging habits without assuming that drivers
arrive with empty batteries or always leave fully charged. For scale, U.S. references
report 19.9 driving miles per day and a median model-year-2024 EV range of 283 miles
\cite{Driving2024,Range2024}. Using these as external reference values gives
$\nu_i\approx0.492q_i/\delta_i$ visits per week. The public-use share and typical
recharge fraction still determine the local estimate; a national driving average and
a new-vehicle range are not measurements of Springfield's fleet.

\subsection{Peak and Off-Peak Arrival Rates}
\label{sec:arrival-rates}
Weekly volume alone cannot reveal congestion: the same visits
may be spread across the week or concentrated in a few hours. We therefore divide the
week into peak windows $P_i$ with total duration $H_i$ hours and an off-peak period
of $168-H_i$ hours. We assume the public ports are available throughout the week.
Let $p_i$ be the fraction of weekly visits arriving during peak hours. The incoming
rate $\lambda_{i,y}(h)$, measured in vehicles per hour at weekly time $h$, is
\begin{equation}
\lambda_{i,y}(h)=
\begin{cases}
V_{i,y}p_i/H_i,&h\in P_i,\\
V_{i,y}(1-p_i)/(168-H_i),&h\notin P_i.
\end{cases}\label{eq:arrivals}
\end{equation}
This expression translates weekly demand into the time-varying input needed to estimate
queue buildup and recovery. Constant rates within each block retain the main peak
pattern with few parameters, while preserving the total weekly volume $V_{i,y}$.
The windows retain their actual positions in the week; queues continue between them.

Peak windows and visit shares can be estimated from normalized session-start counts
for comparable residential, workplace, and commercial facilities
\cite{NorwayCharging,NRELWorkplace,KoreaCharging2024}. The same records provide
port-occupation durations. We use matching venue and charger types; these timing
profiles do not determine local visit frequency. Only the selected profile's peak
windows, peak share, and duration distribution are needed in the service calculation.

\subsection{Queuing Model: Waiting and Completed Service}
\label{sec:queue}
Charging demand becomes a queue when every available port is occupied. Additional
ports can reduce this delay, but a limited construction budget may leave some districts
overloaded during busy hours. We therefore compare the waiting caused by each feasible
capacity, including capacities that cannot immediately serve every peak.

\textbf{Arrivals and service.} We model each district as one first-come, first-served
queue with $c_i$ parallel charging ports. Pooling ports assumes that customers can use
the available facilities within their district; it approximates their combined capacity
without modeling individual station catchments. An arriving vehicle starts charging
if a port is free and otherwise joins the queue. It leaves the service system when
it releases the port. Vehicles do not abandon the waiting queue.

Arrivals follow a Poisson process with the piecewise constant rate in
Equation~\ref{eq:arrivals}. This assumes independent arrivals within each time block.
For a block of length $\Delta h$ hours at rate $\lambda$, the number of arrivals satisfies
\begin{equation}
N(\Delta h)\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda\Delta h).
\label{eq:poisson}
\end{equation}
The distribution allows actual arrivals to fluctuate around the expected number,
so even moderate average demand can occasionally produce a queue.

Each visit occupies a port for a random duration $D_i$, sampled independently from
a duration distribution appropriate to the venue and charger type. The mean duration
$\tau_i=\E[D_i]$ determines the average handling rate per continuously occupied port:
\begin{equation}
\mu_i=\frac{1}{\tau_i},\qquad
K_i=c_i\mu_i,\qquad
\rho_i(h)=\frac{\lambda_{i,y}(h)}{K_i}\quad(c_i>0).
\label{eq:handling}
\end{equation}
Here $K_i$ is the average full-load handling capacity in vehicles per hour. Comparing
incoming demand with $K_i$ reveals when queues tend to grow. A peak with $\rho_i>1$
brings vehicles faster than fully occupied ports can serve them. An off-peak period
with $\rho_i<1$ provides spare capacity to clear accumulated demand, although random
arrivals can still cause waiting. A district with no ports completes no visits.

For illustration, four ports with a mean occupation time of two hours can handle
an average of two vehicles per hour when continuously occupied. A sustained arrival
rate of three vehicles per hour exceeds that capacity; a later rate of one vehicle
per hour leaves capacity to reduce the backlog. The amount of waiting depends on
how long both periods last, as well as their rates.

This is a time-varying $M_t/G/c$ queue: $M_t$ denotes Poisson arrivals with a changing
rate, $G$ a general service-duration distribution, and $c$ parallel ports
\cite{LarsonOdoni}. Exponential service durations give the special case $M_t/M/c$;
Poisson arrival counts do not imply Poisson service durations. We retain the general
duration model so that selecting a distribution can follow the charging records.
Occupation lasts until the port is released, including connected time after active
charging where that is recorded.

\textbf{Queue simulation.} Process visits in arrival order. For each visit, record
its arrival, the time a port becomes available, its service start, and its release
after duration $D_i$. Waiting is the interval between arrival and service start.
The queue and occupied ports carry forward from peak to off-peak hours and across
days. Repeating the simulation estimates expected waiting and completed visits.
This transient calculation accommodates temporary overload; it does not require a
steady-state waiting formula or assume that queues disappear when a peak ends.

\textbf{A common comparison period.} Every candidate capacity is evaluated over the
same interval of $T$ hours, covering the same parts of the week, with a common specified
initial queue and occupied-port state. This makes differences in waiting attributable
to construction rather than different observation periods. The measurement period
$T$ and the 2025--2030 investment horizon are separate: one measures service, while
the other identifies possible opening dates. The chosen $T$ and initial state are
required inputs to a numerical comparison.

Let $Q_{i,y}(u)$ be the number waiting at time $u$ in the comparison period. Define
\begin{equation}
W_{i,y}(T)=\E\!\left[\int_0^T Q_{i,y}(u)\,du\right],\qquad
B_{i,y}(T)=\E[Q_{i,y}(T)].\label{eq:waiting}
\end{equation}
The area under the queue counts all vehicle-hours spent waiting, including the waiting
already experienced by vehicles still in line at the end. This is the burden that
additional ports reduce. For example, ten vehicles waiting for half an hour contribute
five vehicle-hours. The terminal backlog $B_{i,y}$ records unfinished demand and must
be reported alongside waiting; the end of observation does not remove those requests.
A simulation continued into another period carries its remaining queue and occupied ports.

\textbf{Charging revenue.} Let $S_{i,y}(T)$ be the expected completed visits in the
same period and $r_i$ the average receipt per completed visit. Then
\begin{equation}
\mathcal R_{i,y}(T)=r_iS_{i,y}(T).\label{eq:revenue}
\end{equation}
Charging frequency affects incoming demand, while the queue determines how much of it
can be completed and earn revenue. Once ports are saturated, more arrivals may increase
waiting without increasing receipts. For energy-based billing, $r_i$ reflects the mean
energy delivered per visit; frequent small charges need not earn more than fewer large
ones. Annual financial tests use annual completed visits, rather than treating the
receipts from a shorter observation period as a full year's revenue.

\subsection{TOPSIS Construction Utility}
\label{subsec:topsis}
We score each construction configuration using waiting saved and additional charging
revenue. For district $i$ in year $y$, compare configuration $\ell$ with no new construction,
using the same demand, observation period, and initial state:
\begin{equation}
b_{i,y,1}(\ell)=W_{i,y}(0)-W_{i,y}(\ell),\qquad
b_{i,y,2}(\ell)=\mathcal R_{i,y}(\ell)-\mathcal R_{i,y}(0).
\label{eq:benefits}
\end{equation}
Here the argument denotes the construction choice and the common $T$ is suppressed.
Benefits are calculated for the combined ports in a district, so two stations cannot
each claim the same reduction in waiting or the same customer receipts.

TOPSIS converts these two benefits into a comparable construction score
\cite{Hwang1981}. Let $L_j,H_j$ be the minimum and maximum for criterion $j$ over all
evaluated districts, years, and configurations, including no-build baselines. With
positive criterion weights $\omega_1+\omega_2=1$, set
\begin{equation}
v_{i,y,j}=\omega_j\frac{b_{i,y,j}-L_j}{H_j-L_j},\qquad
D^+=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^2(v_{i,y,j}-\omega_j)^2},\qquad
D^-=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^2v_{i,y,j}^2}.
\label{eq:normalize}
\end{equation}
The resulting score is
\begin{equation}
U_{i,y}=100\frac{D^-}{D^++D^-}.\label{eq:topsis}
\end{equation}
The same weights and reference ranges apply to every schedule; a larger score means
greater construction utility under those choices. A constant criterion is omitted;
if neither criterion varies, all alternatives tie. District priority is assessed using
the same added capacity in each district, while the schedule search uses actual site
capacities and costs.

\subsection{Citywide EV Registration Forecast}
\label{sec:forecast}

The deployment roadmap in Task~3 depends on knowing when demand will exceed installed charger capacity. This section forecasts citywide EV registrations through 2030, with particular attention to 2025--2027 as required by Task~1c. We compute an ARIMA time-series model as the primary method and a logistic S-curve as a technology-diffusion baseline.

\subsubsection{ARIMA vs. Logistics modeling}
The ARIMA model describes a time series using its own past values (autoregressive terms) and past errors (moving-average terms), imposing no predetermined shape. The Augmented Dickey--Fuller test fails to reject a unit root in the level and first difference, so we difference twice and set $d = 2$. With $C_t$ the registrations in year $t$ and $\nabla^2 C_t = C_t - 2C_{t-1} + C_{t-2}$, the general model is

\begin{equation}
\nabla^d C_t = \phi_1 \nabla^d C_{t-1} + \cdots + \phi_p \nabla^d C_{t-p} + \epsilon_t + \theta_1 \epsilon_{t-1} + \cdots + \theta_q \epsilon_{t-q},
\label{eq:arima}
\end{equation}

where $\epsilon_t$ is white noise. Selecting $p, q \in \{0,1\}$ by minimum AIC yields ARIMA$(1,2,0)$ with AIC $= 52.07$, $\hat{\phi}_1 = 0.935$, and residual standard deviation $79$ vehicles.

Figure~\ref{fig:acf-pacf} shows the second-differenced series with its ACF and PACF. Because only four second-differenced observations are available, partial autocorrelations can be estimated at lag~1 only. Both lag-1 values fall within the 95\% significance bounds, consistent with the ARIMA$(1,2,0)$ specification though not strong evidence for it; diagnostics have limited power on such a short series.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\IfFileExists{ev_arima_acf_pacf.png}{\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{ev_arima_acf_pacf.png}}{\AcfOriginal{0.95\textwidth}}
\caption{Second-differenced EV registration series (left) with its ACF (center) and PACF (right). With only four second-differenced observations, lag-1 values are the only estimable ones.}
\label{fig:acf-pacf}
\end{figure}

A pure ARIMA has no saturation ceiling, so we impose a conservative business upper bound of 25{,}000 vehicles, well above the 2030 forecast. This cap binds only the distant tail and does not affect the near-term projections.

The logistic model is the classic technology-diffusion curve, assuming growth starts slowly, accelerates, and saturates at a carrying capacity $K$:

\begin{equation}
C_t = \frac{K}{1 + e^{-r(t - t_0)}},
\label{eq:logistic}
\end{equation}

where $r$ is the growth rate and $t_0$ the inflection point. Fitting this curve to the same data provides a useful upper-bound scenario. We do not adopt it as the primary forecast, because the short series shows no clear evidence of saturation, and the imposed S-shape may overstate long-run growth.

\subsubsection{Forecast Comparison}
\label{subsec:forecast-compare}

Figure~\ref{fig:ev-forecast} overlays the historical data, the ARIMA forecast with its 95\% interval, the logistic baseline, and the 25{,}000-vehicle cap. Table~\ref{tab:forecast-compare} lists the point forecasts. The two models agree closely through 2026, then diverge: the logistic curve reaches 14{,}751 vehicles by 2030, while ARIMA reaches 11{,}915. The ARIMA uncertainty band widens over time but remains below the logistic curve. The service model uses these forecasts as demand inputs; expansion years depend on public charging frequency, port occupation and financial viability.

We adopt ARIMA as the primary forecast for three reasons. Its residuals satisfy the assumptions of statistical inference, whereas the logistic curve imposes an unsupported saturation shape. It follows the recent trend without forcing an early inflection, making it more conservative for public investment. The two models also produce similar near-term forecasts (2025--2027). Their effect on revised expansion dates still requires the independent capacity inputs. The logistic curve is retained as an optimistic upper scenario for subsequent sensitivity analysis.

The forecast provides the registered-EV input for the local demand calculation in
Section~\ref{sec:weeklycapacity}. Financial break-even is assessed in
Section~\ref{subsec:break-even} before the joint schedule search.

\subsection{Future District Demand and Capacity}
\label{sec:weeklycapacity}
To apply the citywide forecast to local queues, we assume each district retains its
2024 share of registrations. Separate district adoption histories are unavailable,
so this preserves the observed geographical distribution while allowing the fleet to grow:
\begin{equation}
E_{i,y}=E_{i,2024}\frac{C_y}{2180}.\label{eq:district-growth}
\end{equation}
Together with Equation~\ref{eq:visits}, this raises expected visits to approximately
1.49 times the 2024 level in 2025 and 5.47 times that level by 2030, holding charging
habits fixed. The forecast therefore changes both waiting and the number of potential
paying visits used to evaluate construction.

The construction phases are 2025--2026, 2027--2028, and 2029--2030. Let $z_s\in\{0,1,2,3\}$
identify the opening phase of site $s$, with zero meaning unbuilt. We assume each selected
site opens at the start of its phase with its listed maximum capacity and remains open.
For phase $t(y)$ containing year $y$, the available ports in district $i$ are
\begin{equation}
c_i(y;z)=c_i^0+\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_i}M_s\ind\{1\le z_s\le t(y)\}.
\label{eq:capacity}
\end{equation}
Here $\mathcal S_i$ contains that district's candidate sites and $M_s$ is the number of
ports added by site $s$. This expression sends each candidate schedule's capacity
into the queue model, where it determines handling capacity $c_i(y;z)\mu_i$.

\subsection{Financial Break-Even and Investment Viability}
\label{subsec:break-even}\label{sec:expansion}\label{sec:finance-link}
Financial viability screens proposed investments before schedules are compared.
The break-even calculation measures the business needed to cover annualized installation
and maintenance costs.

A station breaks even when the revenue it collects from the EVs it serves covers its
annualized cost. Let $c_s$ be the installation cost and $m_s$ the annual maintenance cost
of site $s$. Amortizing installation over a ten-year horizon at $\alpha=0.1$, and assuming
each EV contributes $R=\$50$ per year in charging revenue, the break-even number of EVs is

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{BE}_s = \frac{\alpha\, c_s + m_s}{R} = \frac{0.1\, c_s + m_s}{50}.
\end{equation}

Table \ref{tab:breakeven} reports $\mathrm{BE}_s$ for every site. The lowest threshold is 740 EVs at S6; the most expensive site, S9, needs 1,600.

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\textbf{Charging frequency and annual receipts.} The $\$50$ benchmark can be related
to charging habits. Under stable annual demand, let $\eta_i$ be the fraction of requested
public visits completed. Annual receipts per registered EV are then
\begin{equation}
R_i^{\rm EV}=52\nu_i\eta_i r_i.\label{eq:annual-receipt}
\end{equation}
Thus frequency affects potential annual revenue, and service capacity affects the
fraction collected. The benchmark represents $52\nu_i\eta_i r_i=50$. Where queues
continue growing, annual receipts are calculated from actual simulated annual
completions; a short peak-period completion count is not extrapolated into annual income.

\textbf{Later investment condition.} Only Phase~1 has a fixed spending cap. For a group
$G$ of proposed later additions in the same district, annual incremental receipts must
cover their annualized installation, maintenance, and additional operating costs:
\begin{equation}
\Delta\Pi_{G,y}=\Delta\mathcal R^{\rm ann}_{G,y}-\Delta O^{\rm ann}_{G,y}
-\sum_{s\in G}(0.1c_s+m_s)\ge0.
\label{eq:viability}
\end{equation}
The revenue difference compares the proposed configuration with the same district
without those additions, holding other openings fixed. $\Delta O^{\rm ann}$ includes
variable expenses not already counted in maintenance. We apply this annualized test
in the opening year and subsequent evaluated years. It is the financial screen for
later phases, rather than a second budget limit. Joint additions in Downtown are
assessed together to avoid assigning the same customers to both stations.

\section{Joint Station and Construction Schedule Selection}
\label{sec:selection}
\subsection{Candidate Sites and Cost}
\label{subsec:site-attributes}
The candidate sites convert a demand priority into a concrete investment. Each site
adds a specified number of ports and incurs installation and annual maintenance costs.
We assume the listed candidates are the feasible decision set and their quoted costs
and capacities are accurate, as supplied by the problem. Table~\ref{tab:sites} gives
these inputs; each selected station adds its listed maximum number of ports.
\begin{table}[htbp]\centering\small
\caption{Candidate site inputs; monetary values are in \$10,000.}\label{tab:sites}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrr@{}}\toprule
Site&District&Installation&Annual maint.&Ports&Land\\\midrule
S1&Downtown&45&2.5&10&3\\
S2&Downtown&38&2.0&8&4\\
S3&Northside&30&1.8&6&5\\
S4&Southside&28&1.5&6&4\\
S5&Eastside&32&1.8&6&5\\
S6&Westside&25&1.2&4&5\\
S7&University&35&2.0&8&3\\
S8&Industrial&40&2.2&10&4\\
S9&Mall District&50&3.0&12&2\\
S10&Riverside&35&1.8&6&5\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}\end{table}

\textbf{Land scarcity.} Scarce land can increase acquisition, leasing, or site-preparation
expense. The supplied 1--5 land-availability score indicates relative availability,
not a price per unit area. We use the quoted installation cost as the base project
cost and flag low-availability sites for land confirmation. Any documented land expense
not already included must be added to the investment cost (or annual maintenance for
a lease) before selection and break-even analysis. An arbitrary dollar surcharge from
the ordinal score would create cost information absent from the problem.

Downtown has two candidates. Its four capacity configurations are 12 existing ports,
22 with S1, 20 with S2, and 30 with both. We evaluate each combined configuration
against the same local demand. The second station's benefit is the improvement beyond
what the first already supplies, preventing double counting of customers and waiting
savings. Every other district has one candidate addition.

\subsection{Phase-1 Selection Constraints}
Using the opening-phase choices $z_s$ defined above, the first phase must satisfy
\begin{equation}
\sum_{s=1}^{10}c_s\ind\{z_s=1\}\le2{,}000{,}000,\qquad
4\le\sum_{s=1}^{10}\ind\{z_s=1\}\le6.
\label{eq:phaseone}
\end{equation}
These conditions enforce the initial appropriation and the required station count.
Only Phase~1 has a fixed budget. Subsequent construction is governed by financial
benefit, not additional phase budgets. Candidate sites must also have confirmed land
and access; the land score is retained for that assessment rather than used as an
unsupported numerical exclusion threshold.

We interpret the requirement for at least one station in each district as a terminal
coverage goal. Nine districts cannot all receive a new station within the Phase-1
limit of four to six sites, so coverage is required by the end of Phase~3:
\begin{equation}
\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_i}\ind\{z_s>0\}\ge1\qquad(i=1,\ldots,9).
\label{eq:coverage}
\end{equation}
This interpretation reconciles the two requirements. If coverage and later financial
viability cannot both be satisfied, the feasible set is empty; profitability is not
assumed merely to force a solution.

\subsection{Station Connectivity Graph Analysis}
\label{subsec:connectivity}
Following Task~2-c, we treat the symmetric distance matrix as driving distances between
district centroids. Districts are nodes, and an edge joins two districts whose supplied
distance is at most five miles. With $d_{ij}$ the distance, the adjacency and degree are
\begin{equation}
A_{ij}=\ind\{i\ne j,\ d_{ij}\le5\},\qquad k_i=\sum_j A_{ij}.
\label{eq:graph}
\end{equation}
The graph describes geographical connectivity and identifies highly connected districts;
it does not reassign charging demand to another district.
\begin{table}[htbp]\centering\small
\caption{Five-mile district connectivity.}\label{tab:connectivity}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lp{0.56\textwidth}r@{}}\toprule
District&Neighbors&Degree\\\midrule
Downtown&Southside, Eastside, University, Mall District&4\\
Northside&Westside, University&2\\
Southside&Downtown, Industrial&2\\
Eastside&Downtown, University, Mall District&3\\
Westside&Northside, Riverside&2\\
University&Downtown, Northside, Eastside, Mall District&4\\
Industrial&Southside&1\\
Mall District&Downtown, Eastside, University&3\\
Riverside&Westside&1\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}\end{table}

The graph contains eleven edges and one connected component. Downtown and University
tie for the highest degree, while Industrial and Riverside each have one neighbor.
Thus a geographically central district need not be the district with the greatest
waiting reduction: centrality and local service benefit answer different questions.

To test a requirement for an early station in a maximum-degree district, repeat the
schedule search with at least one of S1, S2, or S7 opening in Phase~1. The difference
between the unrestricted best utility and the restricted best utility measures the
benefit forgone by imposing that geographical requirement. If a best schedule already
satisfies it, the difference is zero. The comparison uses the same demand, weights,
and costs as the main selection.
\subsection{Exhaustive Schedule Selection}
\label{sec:schedules}
Each of the ten sites has four choices: Phase~1, Phase~2, Phase~3, or unbuilt.
We therefore enumerate at most $4^{10}=1,048,576$ complete schedules. This single search
determines both the selected locations and every opening phase.

For each schedule $z$, calculate the yearly port counts from Equation~\ref{eq:capacity}
and evaluate waiting savings and additional revenue under the corresponding forecast
demand. Combine the district TOPSIS benefits across planning years:
\begin{equation}
F(z)=\sum_{y=2025}^{2030}\beta_y\sum_{i=1}^{9}
\bigl[U_{i,y}(z)-U_{i,y}(0)\bigr],\qquad
z^*=\underset{z\in\mathcal F}{\arg\max}\ F(z).
\label{eq:schedule-objective}
\end{equation}
$\mathcal F$ contains schedules satisfying the Phase-1 budget and station count,
terminal district coverage, site feasibility, and the financial condition for later
additions. The nonnegative weights $\beta_y$ state the importance assigned to each
year; equal weights value years equally. $U_{i,y}(0)$ is the no-new-construction
baseline. All capacities already open in a district are evaluated together, so their
benefits are counted once.

The search proceeds as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Enumerate opening-phase choices and discard schedules that violate the initial
budget, station count, or terminal coverage.
\item Evaluate queue performance and annual receipts for each remaining schedule,
using common arrival and service samples when comparing alternatives. Reject later
additions that fail the financial condition.
\item Calculate $F(z)$ with the same TOPSIS weights and reference ranges throughout.
Choose its maximum, breaking ties by lower total installation cost.
\end{enumerate}
The resulting $z^*$ specifies the complete three-phase construction schedule.
